extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and professionals (general practitioners, medical jurists, engineers, geologists, science educators)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted standards and practical criteria spanning (a) medical/forensic verification of death and explanations for postmortem phenomena, (b) pedagogical practice for teaching practical chemistry, (c) engineering surveying/excavation and tunneling practices, and (d) observational/mineralogical methods for volcanic study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-lab pedagogy: provide apparatus and clear directions
rubrics_metrics.description: Give students simple apparatus and clear directions so they can do chemical testing by themselves; construct a small laboratory that can be furnished to anybody by the instrument-maker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author reports success from supplying only simple apparatus and 'clear directions' and allowing pupils to perform tests independently; emphasizes furnishing means of practice to secure advantages of self-instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence of instruction: theory then table-practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary study of theoretical chemistry for months before practical analytical exercises, followed by table-practice sessions (example: seven months theory, then eight weeks table-practice / twenty-four school-hours, with many students voluntarily adding hours).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reported effective regimen: extended theoretical grounding (regular recitations) combined with concentrated practical periods; practical experience rapidly supplies needed elementary conceptions and increases interest and effectiveness of reading/theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow entire freedom during practical work
rubrics_metrics.description: Students 'are allowed entire freedom while at work' — giving freedom of action during practical laboratory exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freedom promotes self-instruction, sense of conquest, voluntary extra effort, and pleasurable pursuit; instructor furnishes apparatus/directions but permits independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate success by timed practical examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure practical skill by timed analyses under exam conditions (example: 50 analyses by 14 students in a little over one hour with 'not a single failure').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examination performance is presented as proof of the method's effectiveness; use random samples and timed laboratory analysis to assess competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward unverified historical case reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Question credibility of earlier writers and popular accounts on rare phenomena (e.g., premature burials), and require particulars by which accuracy can be tested before accepting cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taylor and the author reject many reported cases because they lack testable particulars or come from unreliable sources; emphasize careful evidence evaluation and skepticism toward sensational claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal/administrative precaution: morgues and burial-delay laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Many countries require the lapse of twenty-four hours or longer between death and burial, and maintain morgues/dead-houses where slight movements are observed — though some authorities deem them superfluous if ordinary care by relatives is taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Morgues and legal waiting periods are institutional safeguards against premature burial; but competent authorities argue these may be unnecessary when proper medical verification and care occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary verification: listen for heart-beat for sufficient intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: When a medical practitioner 'does his duty' he must call to his aid ordinary means as taught in medical schools, 'of listening at proper intervals and for a sufficient length of time for the heart-beat' — the heart will not remain in perfect repose for five minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prolonged, careful auscultation is the principal test to distinguish trance from death; claims of extended suspension of heart action are considered due to negligent or imperfect tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respiratory detection: mirror or dish on chest to note movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Respiratory movements can be noted by placing a piece of looking-glass, or a dish filled with water or mercury, upon the chest and allowing light to be reflected on the surface — slightest movement produces oscillations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple, non-invasive visual test is recommended for non-medical observers to detect respiratory movement and help verify death versus suspended animation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiological limit: impossible to suspend animation undetected for long periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical jurists conclude that it is impossible to suspend animation or simulate the same, without detection by ordinary means, for so long a space of time as one hour; the heart cannot intermit its beats for five minutes in perfect repose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use physiological time-limits as a standard: reported cases of very prolonged suspension are treated skeptically and as likely due to negligent testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware warmth and lack of pallor as deceptive signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Continued or increased warmth of the body and absence of corpse pallor are common mistaken signs; bodies that remained warm for days have been observed (e.g., cholera cases with temperatures 87–92°F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on body temperature or pallor to declare death; use auscultation and respiratory checks to avoid error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postmortem muscular irritability and rigor mortis timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Muscular irritability can persist after death; rigor mortis generally sets in within five or six hours, lasting from sixteen to twenty-four hours; muscles may exhibit contractions and relaxations after death (example: movements up to an hour after cessation in one cholera case; physiologists could excite irritability up to 16 hours postmortem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for postmortem muscular contractions and rigor mortis timeline when interpreting changes of position or apparent motion after death—these phenomena have natural explanations and are not evidence of life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-interment expulsion causes (obstetrical interpretation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported cases of a child found born after interment can be due to either contracting power remaining in the uterus after maternal death or pressure exerted by putrefactive gases — the latter being more frequent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Medical jurists attribute post-interment birth to natural muscular/putrefactive mechanisms rather than resurrection; use obstetrical knowledge and decomposition-related gas pressure in explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for authenticated, well-documented extraordinary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Extraordinary claims (e.g., prolonged trance or resuscitation after burial) require properly authenticated cases with sufficient details to be admissible as evidence; many historical lists (e.g., Fontenelle's forty-six cases) are rejected for insufficient particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain evidentiary standards: accept only cases with reliable documentation and contemporaneous medical observation; treat anecdotal/secondhand reports skeptically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tunnel alignment verification: triangulation and repeated checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative positions of tunnel openings and direction must be calculated from triangulations; independent triangulations (different systems) should give results agreeing closely (example: two series agreeing within two seconds of direction). Observatories, field-glasses, lamps, and periodic verifications (two or three times a year) were used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use redundant surveying methods and periodic re-verification to ensure the tunnel axis is correct; large triangles and practical projection checks increase accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerances achieved in long-tunnel alignment and level
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported tolerances on the St. Gothard Tunnel: actual length about twenty-five feet shorter than calculated; difference in level of the two galleries not more than four inches; lateral deviation not more than eight inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These empirical tolerances illustrate acceptable alignment precision for a long tunnel when careful surveying and verification are used; set comparable tolerances in similar projects as targets or benchmarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer machine boring with compressed-air perforators driven by water-power
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy to dispense with hand-boring as far as possible; machines driven by water-power transmitted into the tunnel by compressed-air apparatus (Colladon system) were used; turbines turned compressors producing 200 horsepower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt mechanized boring to increase speed and efficiency; ensure reliable power sources (water falls/turbines) and appropriate compressor design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed-air management: cooling and staged piping
rubrics_metrics.description: Compressed air (4–8 atmospheres) became very hot and had to be cooled by circulating cold water around pumps and pistons and by injection of fine spray; air was passed through reservoirs to free it from water, then conducted into the tunnel by large tubes reduced in diameter as work advanced to correspond with diminishing air expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design compressed-air systems with cooling and moisture-removal measures; size piping to match pressure losses and changing consumption along tunnel length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and account for air-pressure loss along long conduits
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of pipes upward of sixteen thousand feet in each gallery showed that absolute pressure equivalent to 6.5 atmospheres at the mouth diminished toward the face to as low as 1 1/8 atmospheres; at lower pressure the diameter of perforators had to be enlarged and more air spent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect significant pressure loss over long piping runs; monitor pressures and adjust equipment (e.g., perforator size) and supply accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooling and human endurance: expect high face temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperature at the front of excavations rose to 91° (F) during late operations and greatly taxed the endurance of workmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan ventilation, cooling, and work-rest cycles to manage high temperatures at the excavation face; consider human factors and heat stress mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explosive use and productivity estimate
rubrics_metrics.description: Calculations estimated that, overall, each kilogramme of dynamite used corresponded with a cubic metre of rock removed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such productivity estimates when planning explosive requirements, but verify empirically for local rock conditions; combine explosives with mechanized boring and top-down excavation to improve advance rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excavation method: advance gallery, enlargement, arches, and trenching
rubrics_metrics.description: Borings began by cutting out a gallery about eight feet square at the top of the intended excavation; after advance boring, enlarge on right and left, build roof arches, dig a trench nearly ten feet wide to tunnel base ('dinette de Strosse'), then remove remaining Strosse—most digging done downward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow staged excavation: small advance gallery → side enlargements → roof support/arches → trench to base → remove central mass; adapt where water infiltration, very hard rocks, or loose beds present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate common excavation interferences and hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Work was interfered with by infiltration of water (not affecting dynamite), rocks of exceptional hardness, and beds of loose material dangerous to work in because of risk of mass falling and cutting off retreat; parts of mass fell, causing casualties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for water control, rock-hardness variability, ground-support for loose materials, emergency egress, and worker safety; monitor for collapse risk and implement protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compressed-air flow study opportunity: treat long piping as experimental data
rubrics_metrics.description: The long pipe runs afforded opportunities to study flow of compressed air through metallic conduits; loss of air in passing through pipes was an important factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use large infrastructure projects to collect engineering data on fluid flow and pressure loss; apply learnings to future tunnel perforation design and cost reduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic-product classification for eruption study
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide eruptive products into two categories: (1) volatile matters exhaled as gases and condensible vapors; and (2) lavas overflowing in imperfect fusion, or thrown out as ashes and scoria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this classification as a framework when sampling and analyzing eruption products; track changes in gas/lava composition over eruption stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track gas composition changes during eruption stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Gases varied greatly during eruption: early gases (not yet acted on by air) were rich in combustible elements, particularly free hydrogen; later stages saw combustible elements disappear and variable composition (hydrogen, marsh-gas, hydrochloric, sulphuric and carbonic acids, sulphuretted hydrogen, nitrogen).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct temporal gas analyses during eruptions to understand volatile evolution and infer processes (e.g., water vapor involvement and role in explosions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectroscopic and analytical salt detection at vents
rubrics_metrics.description: Over central eruptive mouths the spectroscope showed volatilized salts of soda and potash; after eruptive manifestations salts deposited around orifices were analyzed and found to include chlorides/sulphates/carbonates of sodium, potassium, magnesia, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spectroscopic observation during high-temperature activity and collect post-eruption deposits for chemical analysis to test hypotheses (e.g., seawater involvement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret absence of ammonia as environmental evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Hydrochlorate of ammonia commonly abundant in eruptions was almost wanting at Santorin; this lends support to the opinion that ammoniacal product of volcanoes is of organic origin and may be brought by atmosphere from cultivated/organic regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider local environmental context (distance from cultivated land, organic sources) when interpreting presence/absence of ammoniacal compounds in volcanic emissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mineralogical sampling and separation techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Use techniques such as powerful electromagnets to extract ferruginous minerals and concentrated hydrofluoric acid to separate harder minerals; adopt new processes when traditional picking is impracticable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt laboratory methods to sample constraints (small size, strong adherence); employ magnetic separation and chemical digestion where mechanical separation fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize two-stage crystallization and microlithic analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Crystallization in recent lavas occurred in two stages: (1) larger crystals (length ~1/50 inch and other dimensions >1/10 of that), and (2) much smaller crystals (microliths) which follow the contour of larger crystals and abound in the glassy groundmass; microliths are revealed by microscopy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply microscopic study to detect microliths and understand rock texture and cooling history; do not assume groundmass is wholly uncrystalline without micrography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of mineral crystallization for lava interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed order of crystallization in the 1866 lava: 1. Magnetic oxide of iron (large crystals); 2. Apatite; 3. Silicated magnesian irons (augite, hypersthene); 4. Feldspars (large crystals); 5. Microlithic titaniferous oxide of iron; 6. Feldspathic microliths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed crystallization sequences to infer cooling, magmatic differentiation, and conditions of formation; compare mineral order across samples for petrogenetic conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ash composition reflects lava fluidity and microlith content
rubrics_metrics.description: Ashes are pulverized lava and their crystallinity depends on lava condition at the time of becoming ash; more fluid lavas yield pumice-like ash, whereas lavas rich in crystals/microliths yield ashes abundant in crystals and microliths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze ash texture/composition to back-infer the physical state of the lava during explosive fragmentation.
